counterexample: Take n = 4, G = triangle on {v1,v2,v3} together with an isolated vertex v4. Then G has 4 vertices and 3 = n-1 edges, and it contains the cycle C = v1v2v3 with |C| = 3 vertices and 3 edges, exactly the situation line 0003 describes. Line 0003 asserts that the graph left after removing the cycle (n-|C| = 1 vertex, n-1-|C| = 0 edges) 'must contain at least |C|+1 connected components', i.e. at least 4 components. But a graph on a single vertex has exactly 1 connected component, so 1 >= 4 is false. The asserted lower bound is refuted; the only bound the vertex/edge count supports is (n-|C|) - (n-1-|C|) = 1 component. (Line 0003 also silently assumes the cycle uses |C| distinct vertices and |C| edges disjointly reusable, and the correct argument needs the removed cycle vertices to be re-attached, not counted as separate components.)
reasoning_summary: The theorem itself is true, but the proof's 'only if' direction rests on a numerically false counting claim. After deleting a cycle C (|C| vertices, |C| edges) from a graph with n vertices and n-1 edges, line 0003 claims the remaining subgraph has at least |C|+1 connected components. The remainder has only n-|C| vertices, so it can have at most n-|C| components; whenever |C|+1 > n-|C| the claim is impossible. Concretely with n=4 and a triangle plus an isolated vertex, the remainder is a single vertex: 1 component, not the claimed >= 4. Since the whole 'only if' argument concludes 'G cannot be connected' from this bound, the step it relies on is refuted. (Separately, line 0005 proves nothing about an arbitrary acyclic G — it merely constructs one particular path graph — but the line 0003 counterexample alone settles the verdict.)
